Well, I... I suppose I'm here because things at work have gotten completely out of hand, and frankly, I need someone to understand what's actually happening before it goes any further. I work in mathematical sciences—specifically, right now, I'm the lead on this major environmental modeling contract. It's a massive project, absolutely huge datasets, thousands of variables predicting ecological shifts, and I’ve been overseeing the primary architecture of the models. But recently, well, not even that recently, over the last several weeks, I’ve realized that the people on that contract are tracking my revisions. 

Every single time I update the code, every commit I make to the repository, they are watching. And it’s not just monitoring, which, you know, you might expect on a secure contract, but they are actively going in behind me and planting errors in the datasets. Deliberate, calculated errors. They’ll alter a floating-point number or shift a parameter just slightly so that the entire model fails when I run the final simulations. It's incredibly insidious. They are doing it specifically to make it look like I can’t lead the work anymore, to make a paper trail suggesting I'm getting sloppy or that I can't handle the mathematics at my age. 

And the frustrating part, the really maddening part, is that my wife just doesn't see it. I try to show her the logs, and she just brushes it off. She and the junior analysts on my team—they keep telling me the exact same thing. They say, "Oh, it’s just version-control mistakes, it’s just a merge conflict when multiple people are working on the server." But you don't just get a perfectly inverted matrix or a manually deleted algorithm by a simple version-control mistake! That takes intent. They are doing it on purpose to push me out, and no one is listening to me about the data integrity, so I just... I had to come in and talk to someone because the pressure of them watching my every keystroke is just... it's constant.

Well, I mean... another explanation? Look, I've spent my entire adult life—nearly forty years—working in mathematical sciences. I know what an accident looks like. I know what a simple human error looks like. When you're dealing with predictive modeling, especially for environmental systems where you have thousands of overlapping variables... sure, mistakes happen. A misplaced decimal, a typo in a string of code, a failure to pull the most recent update from the server before pushing your own... those are mistakes. I've made them, I've corrected them, I've seen junior analysts make them a hundred times. 

But this? This is not that. I am telling you, I am absolutely certain that there is a coordinated effort here. The people on this contract are tracking my revisions. They are watching when I log in, they are waiting for me to commit the code, and then they are going in and planting these very specific, very calculated errors in the datasets. It’s deliberate. It’s designed to make it look like I’m losing my edge, like I can’t lead this work anymore because I’m sixty and they think I’m past my prime. 

And it’s just so incredibly frustrating because I try to explain this, I try to show the proof. I sit down with my wife, and I pull up the logs, and I say, "Look at this timestamp, look at the alteration here, this isn't a random glitch." And she just sighs and tells me it's version-control mistakes. The junior analysts on my team, they say the exact same thing! "Oh, it's just a merge conflict, it's just the server trying to reconcile two different versions." But you don't reconcile a version by perfectly inverting a matrix! You don't accidentally delete an entire algorithm that took three weeks to write! That doesn't just happen because of a server error. It takes a person, sitting at a keyboard, deciding to sabotage the data. So no, I don't think there's another explanation. I know what I'm looking at, and I know they're doing this to push me out.

Hard to follow? No, I... I don't think so. I mean, nobody has ever explicitly said to me, "Your speech is hard to follow." I communicate very clearly. In my line of work, you have to. I have to explain *how* they are doing it, which involves getting into the weeds of the floating-point numbers and the merge protocols. 

So, no, my thinking is perfectly sound. My speech is perfectly clear. If people are having trouble following me, it's because they aren't paying close enough attention to the mathematics, or they just don't want to put in the effort to understand the sheer scale of what's happening to my datasets. I'm just trying to be thorough, you know? Because if I'm not thorough, if I miss one detail, they win. They prove I'm incompetent. And I can't let that happen.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Suspicious? For most of my life? No, no, absolutely not. I mean, look at my career. You don't spend nearly forty years in mathematical sciences, working on massive collaborative predictive modeling contracts, if you're constantly suspicious of every single person you work with. It just doesn't work that way. When I was in my twenties, right out of college—well, I didn't finish the degree, but I got the certifications that mattered—I was working on these early environmental datasets. And you had to trust your team. You had to trust that when the guy next to you handed over his variables, they were clean. And I did! I trusted them. We went out for beers, we talked about the models, we were a team.

Even up until recently, I was never the guy looking over his shoulder. I mean, sure, in any office environment, you have your politics. You have people who want the promotion you're up for, or someone who takes credit for a subroutine you wrote. That's just human nature, that's business. I never thought there was some grand, orchestrated plot against me just because a project manager was a bit of a jerk, you know? I've always been very pragmatic. I look at the facts. 

But this current situation... this is entirely different. This isn't just office politics or me being paranoid. This is a very sudden, very specific, very targeted campaign that only started in the last few months. Before this contract, before they decided I was too old to lead the architecture, I never had these problems. I never had to check the server logs three times a night. I never had to sit down with my wife and try to prove to her that my colleagues were sabotaging my matrices. I used to just do my work, push the code, and go to sleep! 

So, no, I haven't spent my life being suspicious of people's motives. I've spent my life trusting the math and trusting the process. It's only now, because the evidence is literally right there in the version history, that I have to be on guard. If they weren't actively going into my files and deleting algorithms I spent weeks writing, I wouldn't be suspicious at all! I'd just be doing my job. But when you see a perfectly inverted matrix that you know you didn't touch... well, you'd have to be a fool not to be suspicious of that. But it's a reaction to the data, doctor, not some lifelong personality flaw.

Elevated? Irritable for days at a time? No. No, that sounds like a... a biochemical fluctuation that I simply do not experience. My mood, if you want to call it that, is highly regulated. It’s essentially a steady-state system.

The closest I get to elevated is the quiet satisfaction of running a complex simulation and having the output match the predictive model with a margin of error under point zero one percent. That’s a highly satisfying metric, yes, but I’m not throwing a parade or feeling unusually energized for days on end. I just log the result, document the parameters, and move on to the next dataset. I don't have time for manic episodes, doctor. The math requires focus, not... not emotional fireworks.

Once I identify the error, isolate the logic flaw, and patch the vulnerability, the irritation resolves. The system returns to baseline. It's cause and effect. So no, I don't have these multi-day mood swings you're looking for. My emotional state is entirely dictated by the data in front of me, not some random internal weather system. If the data is clean, I am calm. If the data is being manipulated, I am appropriately vigilant. It really is that simple.
